description_en: A two-storied water reservoir from the 14th-15th century.The monument is located on the side of a path connecting Chipur to Deval Divyapur, at approximately 500 meters north-west of Chipur.The monument consists in a water tank in the ground floor, with an access door and resting platforms to the west, and a "resting room " in the upper floor, accessed from the south. The layout of the ground floor is similar to that of other water tanks built in Ajayamerukoṭa (3 kilometers to the south). The reservoir is accessed by passing through a short vestibule, flanked on each side by a platform with a pillar. Inside, the reservoir is made by receding narrow stone steps. Water is delivered from two carved stone spouts. The ceiling is constituted of a single slabs with a rosette carved in the centre. The slab is supported on the four corners of the room by uncarved spandrels. The two pillars at the entrance of the reservoir are carved with anthropomorphic motifs.The upper room is unseen on other water tanks of Ajayamerukoṭa.. It may be identified as a resting place. Its ceiling is built in the corbelled dome technic. The top slab is decoracted with a carved rosette. On top of the building is a short colonne topped by a a largeāmalakadisc. Thisāmalakadisc may be original to the building, as well it may come from aśikharatemple.Two meters to the south, between masoned terraces, is another, though small, water reservoir.It is difficult to estimate the antiquity of the monument. According to D. R. Sharma, it is locally said that a certain Hati Bhāt built the reservoir "during the time of Nāga Malla of Doti state in the 14th century" and that the wife of Hati Bhāt built another reservoir nearby, the whereabouts of which are unknown (Sharma 2012, p. 321-323). This dating indeed corresponds to the time when similar water structures were built in Ajayamerukoṭa.
references: REFERENCES Sharma, Dilli Raj. 2012. Heritage of Western Nepal. Art and Architecture . Kathmandu: Centre for Nepal and Asian Studies.
